title: Adding and Multiplying Complex Numbers
short: Treat i like a variable, then replace i² with −1.
trouble: Students leave i² in the answer or replace it with +1.

blocks.html: A complex number is written $a + bi$: a real part $a$ and an imaginary part $b$. You add and multiply them with the algebra you already know from multiplying binomials, plus one new fact from The Imaginary Unit i: $i^2 = -1$.

Treat $i$ like a variable: combine real parts with real parts and $i$ terms with $i$ terms. When you multiply, every $i^2$ becomes $-1$, which turns that term real. Always finish in the form $a + bi$.

Complex numbers follow the same rules as polynomials in $i$ (commutative, associative, distributive). So $(2 + 3i) + (4 - i)$ works just like $(2 + 3x) + (4 - x)$. The only difference shows up in multiplication: an $x^2$ term would stay, but $i^2$ is the number $-1$. In the plane, adding complex numbers adds arrows tip to tail, exactly like adding vectors.

blocks.cap: Adding complex numbers adds their arrows tip to tail. Switch to "mul" to see that multiplying turns and stretches.

blocks.title: A number times its conjugate
blocks.a: $25$, a real number. In general $(a + bi)(a - bi) = a^2 + b^2$.

blocks.html: Leaving $i^2$ in the answer, or replacing it with $+1$. In $(2 + 3i)(4 - i)$ the last product is $3i \cdot (-i) = -3i^2 = -3(-1) = +3$. If you got $8 - 3 + 10i = 5 + 10i$, you used $i^2 = 1$. A quick check: $|2 + 3i|^2 \cdot |4 - i|^2 = 13 \cdot 17 = 221$, and $11^2 + 10^2 = 221$ too.
